items.readable_text:
Content:
We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] Now, suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] Can we use integration by parts in this case?

Content:
Let's try. We define [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] as follows:
[MATH: u = x^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = 2x,; (dv)/(dx) = e^{4x}|⟹v = ∫e^{4x}dx = (1)/(4)e^{4x}.]

Content:
So the formula for integration by parts leads to
[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{4x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x^{2}((1)/(4)e^{4x}) − ∫((1)/(4)e^{4x})2xdx; = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)∫xe^{4x}dx.]

Content:
We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take
[MATH: u = x|⟹(du)/(dx) = 1,; (dv)/(dx) = e^{4x}|⟹v = ∫e^{4x}dx = (1)/(4)e^{4x}.]

Content:
Now, integration by parts gives
[MATH: ∫xe^{4x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x((1)/(4)e^{4x}) − ∫((1)/(4)e^{4x}) ⋅ 1dx; = (1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(4)((1)/(4)e^{4x}) + C_{1}; = (1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(16)e^{4x} + C_{1},]
where [MATH: C_1] is a constant of integration.
So we have
[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{4x}dx|= (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)∫xe^{4x}dx; = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)((1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(16)e^{4x} + C_{1}); = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(8)xe^{4x} + (1)/(32)e^{4x} − (C_{1})/(2); = (1)/(32)e^{4x}(8x^{2} − 4x + 1) + C]
where [MATH: C = -\dfrac{C_1}{2}.]

items.title: Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

sections.normalized_html:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

[MATH: u = x^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = 2x; (dv)/(dx) = e^{2x}|⟹v = ∫(dv)/(dx)dx = ∫e^{2x}dx = (e^{2x})/(2).] Using the formula of integration by parts, we get [MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{2x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = (x^{2})((e^{2x})/(2)) − ∫((e^{2x})/(2))(2x)dx; = (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − ∫xe^{2x}dx.]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\int xe^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x.] We take

[MATH: u = x|⟹(du)/(dx) = 1; (dv)/(dx) = e^{2x}|⟹v = ∫(dv)/(dx)dx = ∫e^{2x}dx = (e^{2x})/(2).] In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives [MATH: ∫xe^{2x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x((e^{2x})/(2)) − ∫((e^{2x})/(2))(1)dx; = (xe^{2x})/(2) − (1)/(2)∫e^{2x}dx; = (xe^{2x})/(2) − (e^{2x})/(4) + D] where [MATH: D] is an integral constant.

So we have

[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{2x}dx|= (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − ((xe^{2x})/(2) − (e^{2x})/(4) + D); = (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − (xe^{2x})/(2) + (e^{2x})/(4) + C; = (e^{2x})/(4)(2x^{2} − 2x + 1) + C,] where [MATH: C =-D .]

items.title: Computing the Integral of a Logarithmic Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

key_prerequisites.name: Using Integration by Parts to Calculate Integrals With Logarithms

sections.normalized_html:
We'll work out the indefinite integral first, and then proceed to work out the definite integral.

In this case, we define [MATH: u = (\ln x)^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = (2\ln x)/(x),; (dv)/(dx) = 32x^{3}|⟹v = ∫32x^{3}dx = 8x^{4}.]

Using the formula of integration by parts, we get [MATH: ∫32x^{3}(\ln x)^{2}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = (\ln x)^{2}(8x^{4}) − ∫(8x^{4})((2\ln x)/(x))dx; = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx.]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\int {x^3\ln(x)} \textrm{d}x.] We take [MATH: u = \ln (x)|⟹(du)/(dx) = (1)/(x),; (dv)/(dx) = x^{3}|⟹v = ∫x^{3}dx = (x^{4})/(4).]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives [MATH: ∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = \ln (x)((x^{4})/(4)) − ∫((x^{4})/(4))((1)/(x))dx; = (x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (1)/(4)∫x^{3}dx; = (x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (x^{4})/(16) + C_{1}] where [MATH: C_1] is an integral constant. So, we get that the indefinite integral is [MATH: ∫32x^{3}(\ln x)^{2}dx|= 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx; = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16((x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (x^{4})/(16) + C_{1}); = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 4x^{4}\ln (x) + x^{4} − 16C_{1}; = x^{4}(8(\ln x)^{2} − 4\ln (x) + 1) + C] where [MATH: C = -4C_1.] Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{e}32x^{3}\ln (x)dx|= x^{4}(8(\ln x)^{2} − 4\ln (x) + 1)|_{1}^{e}; = [(e)^{4}(8(\ln (e))^{2} − 4\ln (e) + 1)] − [(1)^{4}(8(\ln (1))^{2} − 4\ln (1) + 1)]; = [e^{4}(8 − 4 + 1)] − 1; = 5e^{4} − 1.]

[MATH: ∫32x^{3}(\ln x)^{2}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = (\ln x)^{2}(8x^{4}) − ∫(8x^{4})((2\ln x)/(x))dx; = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx.]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\int {x^3\ln(x)} \textrm{d}x.] We take
[MATH: u = \ln (x)|⟹(du)/(dx) = (1)/(x),; (dv)/(dx) = x^{3}|⟹v = ∫x^{3}dx = (x^{4})/(4).]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives
[MATH: ∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = \ln (x)((x^{4})/(4)) − ∫((x^{4})/(4))((1)/(x))dx; = (x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (1)/(4)∫x^{3}dx; = (x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (x^{4})/(16) + C_{1}]
where [MATH: C_1] is an integral constant. So, we get that the indefinite integral is
[MATH: ∫32x^{3}(\ln x)^{2}dx|= 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16∫x^{3}\ln (x)dx; = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 16((x^{4}\ln (x))/(4) − (x^{4})/(16) + C_{1}); = 8x^{4}(\ln x)^{2} − 4x^{4}\ln (x) + x^{4} − 16C_{1}; = x^{4}(8(\ln x)^{2} − 4\ln (x) + 1) + C]
where [MATH: C = -4C_1.] Finally then, we can work out the definite integral:

[MATH: ∫_{1}^{e}32x^{3}\ln (x)dx|= x^{4}(8(\ln x)^{2} − 4\ln (x) + 1)|_{1}^{e}; = [(e)^{4}(8(\ln (e))^{2} − 4\ln (e) + 1)] − [(1)^{4}(8(\ln (1))^{2} − 4\ln (1) + 1)]; = [e^{4}(8 − 4 + 1)] − 1; = 5e^{4} − 1.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
We know that we can use the method of integration by parts to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] Now, suppose that we want to calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^2e^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] Can we use integration by parts in this case?

Content:
Let's try. We define [MATH: u] and [MATH: v] as follows:
[MATH: u = x^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = 2x,; (dv)/(dx) = e^{4x}|⟹v = ∫e^{4x}dx = (1)/(4)e^{4x}.]

Content:
So the formula for integration by parts leads to
[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{4x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x^{2}((1)/(4)e^{4x}) − ∫((1)/(4)e^{4x})2xdx; = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)∫xe^{4x}dx.]

Content:
We still don't have an answer, but the problem is reduced to the calculation of a simpler integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int xe^{4x} \textrm{d}x.] To compute this integral, we just need to apply the integration by parts formula again. For this second integral, we take
[MATH: u = x|⟹(du)/(dx) = 1,; (dv)/(dx) = e^{4x}|⟹v = ∫e^{4x}dx = (1)/(4)e^{4x}.]

Content:
Now, integration by parts gives
[MATH: ∫xe^{4x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x((1)/(4)e^{4x}) − ∫((1)/(4)e^{4x}) ⋅ 1dx; = (1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(4)((1)/(4)e^{4x}) + C_{1}; = (1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(16)e^{4x} + C_{1},]
where [MATH: C_1] is a constant of integration.
So we have
[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{4x}dx|= (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)∫xe^{4x}dx; = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(2)((1)/(4)xe^{4x} − (1)/(16)e^{4x} + C_{1}); = (1)/(4)x^{2}e^{4x} − (1)/(8)xe^{4x} + (1)/(32)e^{4x} − (C_{1})/(2); = (1)/(32)e^{4x}(8x^{2} − 4x + 1) + C]
where [MATH: C = -\dfrac{C_1}{2}.]

Item 2 — Example: Computing the Integral of an Exponential Expression Using Integration by Parts Twice

Example Prompt:
Calculate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^2e^{2x}\, \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
We need to use integration by parts.

In this case, we define

[MATH: u = x^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = 2x; (dv)/(dx) = e^{2x}|⟹v = ∫(dv)/(dx)dx = ∫e^{2x}dx = (e^{2x})/(2).]
Using the formula of integration by parts, we get
[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{2x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = (x^{2})((e^{2x})/(2)) − ∫((e^{2x})/(2))(2x)dx; = (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − ∫xe^{2x}dx.]

We use integration by parts once again to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle\int xe^{2x}\,\textrm{d}x.] We take

[MATH: u = x|⟹(du)/(dx) = 1; (dv)/(dx) = e^{2x}|⟹v = ∫(dv)/(dx)dx = ∫e^{2x}dx = (e^{2x})/(2).]
In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives
[MATH: ∫xe^{2x}dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x((e^{2x})/(2)) − ∫((e^{2x})/(2))(1)dx; = (xe^{2x})/(2) − (1)/(2)∫e^{2x}dx; = (xe^{2x})/(2) − (e^{2x})/(4) + D]
where [MATH: D] is an integral constant.

So we have

[MATH: ∫x^{2}e^{2x}dx|= (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − ((xe^{2x})/(2) − (e^{2x})/(4) + D); = (x^{2}e^{2x})/(2) − (xe^{2x})/(2) + (e^{2x})/(4) + C; = (e^{2x})/(4)(2x^{2} − 2x + 1) + C,]
where [MATH: C =-D .]

Evaluate the integral [MATH: \displaystyle \int x^2\cos(3x) \textrm{d}x.]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
In this case, we define
[MATH: u = x^{2}|⟹(du)/(dx) = 2x,; (dv)/(dx) = \cos (3x)|⟹v = ∫\cos (3x)dx = (1)/(3)\sin (3x).]

Using the formula for integration by parts, we get
[MATH: ∫x^{2}\cos (3x)dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = (x^{2})((1)/(3)\sin (3x)) − ∫((1)/(3)\sin (3x))2xdx; = (1)/(3)x^{2}\sin (3x) − (2)/(3)∫x\sin (3x)dx.]

Again, we use integration by parts to evaluate [MATH: \displaystyle \int x\sin(3x) \textrm{d}x.] We take
[MATH: u = x|⟹(du)/(dx) = 1,; (dv)/(dx) = \sin (3x)|⟹v = ∫\sin (3x)dx = − (1)/(3)\cos (3x).]

In this case, the formula for integration by parts gives
[MATH: ∫x\sin (3x)dx|= ∫u(dv)/(dx)dx; = uv − ∫v(du)/(dx)dx; = x(− (1)/(3)\cos (3x)) − ∫(− (1)/(3)\cos (3x)) ⋅ 1dx; = − (1)/(3)x\cos (3x) + (1)/(3)∫\cos (3x)dx; = − (1)/(3)x\cos (3x) + (1)/(3)((1)/(3)\sin (3x)) + C_{1}; = − (1)/(3)x\cos (3x) + (1)/(9)\sin (3x) + C_{1}]
where [MATH: C_1] is a constant of integration.
So we have
[MATH: ∫x^{2}\cos (3x)dx|= (1)/(3)x^{2}\sin (3x) − (2)/(3)∫x\sin (3x)dx; = (1)/(3)x^{2}\sin (3x) − (2)/(3)(− (1)/(3)x\cos (3x) + (1)/(9)\sin (3x) + C_{1}); = (1)/(3)x^{2}\sin (3x) + (2)/(9)x\cos (3x) − (2)/(27)\sin (3x) − (2C_{1})/(3); = (1)/(27)((9x^{2} − 2)\sin (3x) + 6x\cos (3x)) + C,]
where [MATH: C = -\dfrac{2C_1}{3}.]
